Attention, pantry pilgrims: The kettles beat like war drums and the air smells of rosemary and thunder. Doors rattle; shelves murmur; sacks of grain lean to listen. In the hush between ladle and flame, an oath is spoken that tastes like smoke and salt. And from that oath rises the Bean Supreme. They were not crowned in marble halls, but in a village kitchen the night the hearth-guilds failed and winter clawed at every sill. An apprentice cook-witch stirred the Common Pot until the broth sang, traced sigils in steam, and invoked the ancient Legume Rite—Soak, Stir, Share. The beans awoke, each a bright little heartbeat, and the pot swelled with courage; from its brim stepped a figure in a can-crown, bearing the Master Spoon as scepter. Sprouts bent like pennons in a gale; the first oaths were sworn over bread and brine, and the pantry—once a quiet room of keeping—became a chapel of uprising. Word raced along roads and root-cellars alike: hoarded larders were broken, lonely fires rekindled, and the meek were provisioned in the Overlord’s name. The war that followed was brief and boiling. Against the Salt Barons and their iron cauldrons marched millers, picklers, and fieldhands beneath stew-stitched banners; Bigger Beans rolled like sling-stones; the Bean Collective hummed one stout harmony that made sieges feel like supper. By ladle-law the Overlord decreed: No grief in the garden. No false weights at market. No dupe of bread or bean. Consent in spice, kindness in word, and every pot with an off-switch. When the final lid clattered, a Commons Pot was raised at the crossroads—ever-warm, ever-watchful—so travelers might ladle hope without cost. And should famine or foolishness return, the rite endures: strike the Master Spoon thrice on the can-crown, whisper share the beans, and the Overlord will answer—quiet as a simmer, unstoppable as a boil.
